extracted.intended_audience: journalists, communicators, policy advocates, and public-interest storytellers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for framing news and advocacy stories about social issues, contrasting episodic (individual/event-focused) and thematic (context/trend-focused) approaches and their effects on public attribution and policy support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame type — episodic vs thematic
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodic news frames apply a telephoto lens (focusing on individual case studies and discrete events); thematic news frames apply a wide-angle lens (focusing on trends over time and highlighting contexts and environments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction to classify and craft coverage: an episodic frame presents a portrait while a thematic frame presents a landscape. The page emphasizes choosing thematic frames to advance public conversation about social issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus: individual vs issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an episodic frame would focus on an individual, a thematic frame would focus on the issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid anchoring stories solely in a single person's experience if the goal is to show systemic causes or policy solutions. Example: the Reuben Robinson episodic health-care anecdote versus the Endowment for Health’s thematic blueprint report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal focus: single event vs trends over time
rubrics_metrics.description: An episodic frame focuses on a single event; a thematic frame focuses on trends over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To make an issue look public and systemic, include longitudinal data, surveys, or reports showing change or patterns (e.g., school nutrition survey trends vs an isolated overweight-child case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Realm emphasized: private vs public
rubrics_metrics.description: An episodic frame is more likely to keep its focus on the private realm (an individual's psychology or family behaviors); a thematic frame would include the public realm (surrounding environment, public institutions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include institutional, community, or policy-level context to shift interpretation from private failings to public responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem–solution framing: fix the person vs fix the conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodic frames highlight how to fix the person experiencing a problem; thematic frames highlight how to fix the conditions that led to the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for policy change, frame solutions at the systemic or environmental level rather than as individualized remediation. Use examples of recommended systemic remedies (reports, blueprints, stakeholder commitments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience role: consumers vs citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodic frames approach the audience as consumers ('news you can use'); thematic frames approach the audience as citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address readers as stakeholders with civic responsibilities by presenting context and collective implications rather than only actionable tips for individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solution type emphasized: better information vs better policies
rubrics_metrics.description: The solution to problems within an episodic frame is presented as better information for the individual, whereas a thematic frame asks for better policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the objective is structural change, foreground policy recommendations, institutional responsibilities, and collective actions rather than simply educating individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context inclusion — include systems/community-level context
rubrics_metrics.description: Thematic frames identify shortcomings at the community or systems level that have contributed to the problem; episodic frames lack this context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context defines an issue as 'public' and appropriate for policy solutions. Use statistics, reports, stakeholder statements, and descriptions of institutional dynamics (e.g., policy failures, funding shortages) to provide context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution and accountability effects of framing
rubrics_metrics.description: The way an issue is framed affects how people attribute cause and solution: episodic framing makes people less likely to hold government or civic organizations accountable; thematic framing makes people more likely to see the need for collective action and to hold institutions responsible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose framing strategically based on desired public response: to increase support for collective/policy solutions, emphasize thematic elements that point to systemic responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episodic as an anti-pattern: reduces issues to disconnected episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodic frames reduce life to a series of disconnected episodes, random events or case studies, making it difficult to see systemic patterns or public solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when episodic storytelling obscures broader trends; avoid relying solely on isolated anecdotes if the goal is systemic understanding or policy change. The page provides multiple paired examples (healthcare, childhood obesity) showing how episodic anecdotes obscure systemic trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical recommendation: craft and promote thematic stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite media tendency toward episodic stories, communicators can learn to craft and promote compelling thematic stories that bring the public perspective back into the picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use thematic storytelling techniques illustrated in the examples: anchor stories in reports or surveys, quote experts and stakeholders on systemic problems and solutions, summarize blueprints/recommendations, and highlight trends and policy implications rather than only individual narratives.
